📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection.
  • Recent findings suggest that in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm.
  • In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we are excited to open-source PipelineRL, an experimental RL implementation that tackles a fundamental challenge in large-scale Reinforcement Learning with LLMs: the trade-off between inference throughput and on-policy data collection. PipelineRL's key innovation is inflight weight updates during RL training (see Figure 1 below). This allows PipelineRL to achieve constantly high inference throughput and minimize the lag between the weights used for rollouts and the most recently updated model weights. The result: fast and stable RL training for large language models.

Recent findings suggest that in this blog post, we show that 1) inflight weight updates do not harm the training process and 2) PipelineRL achieves competitive results compared to Open-Reasoner-Zero, while using a simpler RL algorithm. We also present the modular PipelineRL architecture that facilitates trying new inference / trainer combinations.

In conventional RL approaches (Figure 1a), there is a trade-off between high throughput inference and on-policy data collection. To explain this trade-off let us first define conventional RL algorithmically:.

To achieve high throughput, the inference servers must use large batch sizes and, therefore, generate data for multiple policy optimization steps. However, each optimization step increases the lag between the current policy and the data collected using the inference policy, progressively making collected data more off-policy and less effective for training. On-policy learning requires data for a single optimization step. But producing small amounts of data with many GPUs is inefficient because this means the per-GPU batch size is small. Furthermore the batch size goes down as the inference server finishes the short sequences and has only the few longest sequences in progress.

PipelineRL (Figure 1b) remediates this trade-off through inflight weight updates. We update the weights in inference servers after each optimizer step without ever stopping inference. We only pause the inference at all inference servers for just the time needed to receive the upcoming weights. Inflight weight updates allow the inference server to constantly maintain the optimal batch size while simultaneously ensuring data remains on-policy or near on-policy, which leads to better GPU utilization and more effective learning, respectively.

To demonstrate the effectiveness of PipelineRL and the benefits of inflight weight updates, we trained a 7B model and 32B model on the Open-Reasoner-Zero dataset. Looking at the learning curves we see that PipelineRL matches or exceeds the performance of Open-Reasoner on the popular reasoning test benchmarks: AIME 2024 and MATH 500 (see Figure 2 above).

Notably, our RL implementation is much simpler than Open-Reasoner-Zero. While Open-Reasoner-Zero uses a value function, our implementation is a simplified version of GRPO. In particular, we found that the trust region importance weight clamping is not needed for stable training. Neither was overlong sequence filtering or reward shaping from the DAPO paper. For normalizing the loss we just use the number of sequences in the batch as the denominator, giving equal weights to all tokens. We used no KL penalty and no entropy bonus (though our implementation does support reference model KL). Despite the simplicity of our implementation, or perhaps thanks to it, training is very stable as you can see in this wandb report.

Sources indicate that one might expect that inflight weight updates would result in an unstable training process, since sequence generation proceeds with stale keys and values in the KV cache that was computed with a previous model version. However, our experiments indicate this does not adversely affect stability.

Sources indicate that pipelineRL is built to be modular and take advantage of rapid improvements in highly-specialized inference and training software (SGLang, vLLM, Nvidia Dynamo, DeepSpeed, FSDP, TorchTitan, FastLLM, etc.). We propose clear contracts between the inference and training components, allowing easy integration of new inference and training solutions as they become available.

The inference software must expose the following APIs to PipelineRL[1]:.

If init_process_group and request_weight_update APIs become the industry standard, one will be able to plug-and-play try using difference inference implementations with PipelineRL.

PipelineRL training code feeds freshly-generated training data to trainer workers as soon as the right number of training tokens has accumulated for each of them. One can make any training software that exposes these Python APIs work with PipelineRL:.

It has been revealed that pipelineRL currently uses the HuggingFace accelerate library to give the user a choice between DeepSpeed and FSDP. But we found that accelerate contract is too flexible and can be confusing. We will be moving to the stricter contract as described above that will make using other trainers easier.

Sources indicate that upcoming features. Our implementation is still experimental and lacks some vital functionality. Top priorities for us include using coroutines for more precise inference batch size control, multi-modal support and sequence parallel training. We would also welcome contributions of more inference server and trainer integrations. We will not, however, try to make the pipeline-rl repo a framework that supports all possible algorithms and reward functions. Our take is that pipeline-rl should be a hackable and fast reference implementation of GRPO with easily verifiable rewards. If you'd like to do a research project using PipelineRL, you can just fork the repo and have fun hacking the code!

Industry observers note that more research coming soon. More analysis is needed to understand how inflight weight updates affect the training dynamics, and to carefully measure the speed-ups that PipelineRL brings. Also, much can be noted about the similarities between PipelineRL and highly relevant prior work on asynchronous Reinforcement Learning for LLMs. For all this and more please stay tuned for our upcoming research paper!

Recent findings suggest that alexandre Piché wrote the first synchronous version of our RL code while working on TapeAgents. Dzmitry Bahdanau refactored the code to be asynchronous and distributed, and implemented inflight weight updates. Rafael Pardinas implemented sequence packing. Ehsan Kamaloo helped with running the experiments. Xiaoyin Chen helped with debugging the framework.

According to recent reports, we acknowledge the prior RL for LLM implementations such as TRL, OpenRLHF and veRL for the many tricks we borrowed from them. Artifacts from other open-source reasoning projects, such as Simple-RL, Deepscaler, DAPO and OpenReasoner were instrumental for stabilizing PipelineRL. We would like to recognize Christopher Manning, Michael Noukhovitch for their thoughtful comments. Finally, we thank the broader ServiceNow Research team and ServiceNow CoreLLM teams for being amazing colleagues.

Breaking: Millions of exploding stars could soon reveal dark energy's secrets

📅 29 Jun 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a new technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.
  • Recent findings suggest that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances.
  • Type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers led by the Institute of Cosmos Sciences of the University of Barcelona (ICCUB) have developed a new technique that could greatly improve how scientists study the expansion of the Universe and investigate the mysterious force known as dark energy.

Recent findings suggest that published in Nature Astronomy, the research introduces a framework called CIGaRS that can extract far more information from Type Ia supernovae, the powerful stellar explosions used to measure vast cosmic distances. Unlike many current approaches, the method relies mainly on imaging data rather than expensive spectroscopic observations. The advance is expected to help astronomers take full advantage of the enormous datasets that will soon arrive from next generation sky surveys, particularly those conducted by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.

Type Ia supernovae occur when white dwarf stars explode. Because these explosions reach nearly the same intrinsic brightness, astronomers use them as "standard candles": by comparing their actual brightness with how bright they appear from Earth, researchers can calculate their distance.

These measurements played a crucial role in the discovery that the Universe is expanding at an accelerating rate. Scientists attribute that acceleration to dark energy, one of the most significant unsolved questions in modern physics.

However, there is an crucial complication. Type Ia supernovae are not perfectly identical.

How Host Galaxies Affect Supernova Measurements.

Over the past 20 years, astronomers have found that a supernova's observed brightness is influenced by the galaxy where it occurs. Supernovae found in older or more massive galaxies can appear slightly different from those occurring in younger or less massive galaxies.

Recent findings suggest that researchers have typically accounted for these differences using relatively simple correction methods. While useful, these approximations can limit the accuracy of distance measurements and, in turn, the precision of cosmological studies.

A Unified Model of Supernovae and the Universe.

Sources indicate that the new framework addresses this challenge by modeling multiple factors simultaneously. Rather than treating each component independently, the researchers built a single, integrated model that includes the supernova explosions themselves, their host galaxies, the dust that alters their light, changes in supernova rates throughout cosmic history, and even the expansion of the Universe.

By connecting all of these ingredients within one statistical and physical framework, the team can capture relationships that are often overlooked when the pieces are analyzed separately.

"A powerful way of modelling the Universe is to simulate it ab initio in the computer using Bayesian inference," says Raúl Jiménez (ICREA-ICCUB), co-author of the study. "This provides a way to vary all possible parameters at the same time to predict what Universe we live in. Furthermore, by having this capacity, one can look into possible 'unknown unknown' systematics to understand their effect. The impact of these systematics in our inference is arguably the most important missing ingredient in current approaches to model the Universe.".

Using Artificial Intelligence To Analyze the Cosmos.

Building such a comprehensive model would normally require enormous computing power. To make the approach practical, the researchers turned to a modern technique called simulation-based inference.

Sources indicate that the process begins with scientists generating large numbers of simulated universes based on physical models. A neural network (a type of artificial intelligence) then learns how the simulated observations relate to the physical properties that produced them. Once trained, the system can compare real astronomical observations with its simulations and determine the most likely underlying parameters.

This strategy makes it possible to analyze tens of thousands of supernovae simultaneously, a task that would be impractical using traditional techniques.

Accurate Galaxy Distances From Images Alone.

One of the study's most significant findings is that the framework can determine galaxy distances (redshifts) with high accuracy using only imaging data.

Redshift measures how much a galaxy's light has been stretched as the Universe expands. It provides information about both the galaxy's distance and how far back in time we are observing it.

According to the researchers, the upcoming method delivers redshift estimates with precision comparable to spectroscopic measurements, but without requiring spectra. This capability is especially important because upcoming surveys are expected to identify millions of supernova candidates, while only a small percentage can realistically receive spectroscopic follow-up observations.

Ready for the Rubin Observatory Data Deluge.

According to recent reports, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, currently being built in Chile, is expected to begin a decade long survey of the sky in the near future. During that mission, it will discover an unprecedented number of supernovae. Roughly 99% of those objects will be observed only photometrically, meaning through images taken in different colors rather than detailed spectra.

The CIGaRS framework was specifically developed with this challenge in mind.

"Unlike other frameworks, which require analytic simplifications, our no-compromise end-to-end simulation-based inference approach is uniquely capable of extracting the full cosmological and astrophysical information from the Rubin Observatory's hard-earned data, while avoiding the pitfalls of selection and modelling biases," states Konstantin Karchev (ICCUB-SISSA Trieste), lead author of the study.

Insights Into How Supernovae Form.

The benefits extend beyond measuring dark energy. The framework also provides new information about the origins of Type Ia supernovae themselves.

By reconstructing how supernova occurrence rates vary with the ages of stars in different galaxies, the model helps scientists investigate long standing questions about the systems that eventually produce these explosions.

In a recent development, the researchers found that combining physics based simulations with artificial intelligence can overcome several limitations of current cosmological methods. They estimate that the approach could improve cosmological constraints by as much as a factor of four compared with traditional techniques that depend only on a relatively small sample of spectroscopically observed supernovae.

As the Rubin Observatory prepares to usher in a new era of astronomical discovery, tools such as CIGaRS could help scientists extract the maximum amount of information from its observations and gain a deeper understanding of the Universe.

Cyberpunk 2’s creative director has joked that the sequel is “cancelled” after seeing what Rockstar has achieved with GTA 6.

GTA 6 has been making quite a splash since its long-awaited release on November 19, with Rockstar’s open-world game becoming the joint best-reviewed game of all time.

It’s so popular that teachers have had to send round a minibus to pick up absent students, while retirement home residents as old as 86 have also been playing.

The hype for GTA 6 has been so enormous that Rockstar reported $3.79 billion in estimated retail sales by the end of its first day, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.

Industry observers note that as you can imagine, this makes GTA 6 a particularly daunting game for other developers looking to follow in its footsteps. This is especially true for Cyberpunk 2 creative director Igor Sarzynski, who joked that it has given him “GTAVI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression.”.

In a November 21 Bluesky post, Sarzynski praised GTA 6’s scale and attention to detail before joking that he was ready to give up game development and rake leaves instead.

It has been revealed that “GTAVI-induced-open-world-game-dev-depression is real. Probably the single greatest artistic achievement in history, I mean it. Scale, density, coherence, thoughtfulness of it all, just a technological and creative miracle. Cyberpunk 2 is cancelled, imma go sweep autumn leaves in my backyard now,” Sarzynski joked.

Despite the daunting task of following up GTA 6 with his own open-world game, Sarzynski remains positive that Cyberpunk 2 will offer fans something different.

Sources indicate that “Seriously though, I think we’re doing something of our own, with a different unique flavor. GTA is impressive in a way all great art is, it expands what is possible, a captivating vision flawlessly executed,” he mentioned.

Cyberpunk 2 currently doesn’t have a release date, but we do know that it’s being made with Unreal Engine 5 and entered pre-production in May 2025.

Introducing AutoRound: Intel’s Advanced Quantization for LLMs and VLMs

📅 29 Apr 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging.
  • AutoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel.
  • Industry observers note that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, as large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) continue to grow in size and complexity, deploying them efficiently becomes increasingly challenging. Quantization offers a solution by reducing model size and inference latency. Intel's AutoRound emerges as a cutting-edge quantization tool that balances accuracy, efficiency, and compatibility.

AutoRound is a weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ) method developed by Intel. It uses signed gradient descent to jointly optimize weight rounding and clipping ranges, enabling accurate low-bit quantization (e.g., INT2 - INT8) with minimal accuracy loss in most scenarios. For example, at INT2, it outperforms popular baselines by up to 2.1x higher in relative accuracy. The image below provides an overview of the core algorithm in AutoRound. For more details, please refer to our paper.

Industry observers note that despite its strong performance, AutoRound is fast and lightweight — quantizing a 72B model takes just 37 minutes on an A100 GPU under light mode. It also supports mixed-bit tuning, lm-head quantization, GPTQ/AWQ/GGUF format exporting, and flexible tuning recipes.

AutoRound delivers highly promising results, particularly in low-bit quantization scenarios. Evaluations across a variety of tasks show that it outperforms popular methods by a wide margin at 2-bit precision (source). At 4 bits, AutoRound continues to hold a competitive edge in most cases, as demonstrated on the Low-Bit Open LLM Leaderboard.

It has been revealed that LLMs: AutoRound supports nearly all popular LLM architectures, including well-known models like Qwen, LLaMA, and DeepSeek. Ready-to-use quantized models are available on Hugging Face through collections such as OPEA, Kaitchup, and fbaldassarri.

In a recent development, VLMs: AutoRound supports over 10 vision-language models (VLMs), including Mistral-Small-3.1, Gemma3, and more. You can find the full list in the README, and ready-to-use quantized models are available in the OPEA Hugging Face collection. For models not yet supported, you can still apply our RTN method with --iters 0. No tuning is required, but some accuracy loss is expected.

AutoRound requires only 200 tuning steps and a small calibration dataset (as few as 128 samples) to achieve high accuracy. This efficiency translates to faster quantization times and reduced resource consumption compared to other int2 methods, which are more computationally intensive.

Right now, only offline mode is supported to generate quantized models.

AutoRound also offers another two recipes, auto-round-best and auto-round-light, designed for optimal accuracy and improved speed, respectively.

According to recent reports, for 2 bits, we recommend using auto-round-best or auto-round. For a comparison of the three recipes, please refer to the table below.

W4G128 Average Accuracy of 13 tasks (mmlu-pro, if_eval, gsm8k, etc) and Time Cost Results (Testing was conducted on the Nvidia A100 80G using the version of PyTorch 2.6.0 with enable_torch_compile):.

This setting offers a better trade-off between accuracy and tuning cost, and is recommended in all scenarios.

For the best/light settings of AutoRound for API usage or mixed-bit configurations, please refer to AutoRound README.

Recent findings suggest that autoRound automatically selects the best available backend based on the installed libraries and prompts the user to install additional libraries when a better backend is found. For more details, please refer to HF README or AutoRound README.

Most GPTQ/AWQ models can be converted to the AutoRound format for better compatibility and support with Intel devices. Please note that the quantization config will be changed if the model is serialized.

Recent findings suggest that autoRound offers a meaningful improvement step forward in post-training quantization for large language and vision-language models. By combining high accuracy, exceptional efficiency, and broad compatibility with popular models, devices, and export formats, AutoRound makes low-bit quantization both practical and powerful. Whether you're deploying LLMs at scale or experimenting with edge inference on VLMs, AutoRound provides the tools and flexibility you need to achieve optimal performance with minimal overhead. We invite you to try it out and join the growing community pushing the boundaries of efficient AI deployment.

According to recent reports, contributions to AutoRound are welcome and greatly appreciated! Whether it's fixing bugs, improving documentation, adding new features, or suggesting improvements, your help is always valued.

If you encounter any problems with auto-round, please open an glitch on the AutoRound repository.

We would like to thank the open-source low-precision libraries including AutoGPTQ, AutoAWQ, GPTQModel, Triton, Marlin and ExLLaMAV2, whose CUDA kernels are used in AutoRound.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for much of the early 20th century, quantum mechanics was one of the most puzzling ideas in science. The theory challenged conventional thinking and left even leading physicists struggling to make sense of its implications. A century later, it has become the foundation of technologies that influence daily life, including lasers, microchips, secure communications, and emerging quantum computers.

In a newly introduced perspective article published in Science, Dr. Marlan Scully of Texas A&M University reflects on the remarkable evolution of quantum mechanics, from an abstract theory about tiny particles to a powerful framework helping researchers tackle some of the most difficult questions in science.

In a recent development, "Quantum mechanics started as a way to explain the behavior of tiny particles," said Scully, who is also affiliated with Princeton University. "Now it's driving innovations that were unimaginable just a generation ago.".

Scully has played a major role in advancing the field. He co-authored the influential textbook Quantum Optics, a resource that has educated generations of physicists. His research in coherent nanoscale laser spectroscopy helped make it possible to study molecules with atomic-scale precision. He has also developed groundbreaking concepts involving quantum heat engines, which challenge traditional assumptions about thermodynamic efficiency and may one day lead to new energy technologies.

From Schrödinger's Cat to Quantum Technology.

Recent findings suggest that one of the most famous illustrations of quantum mechanics came in 1935, when Erwin Schrödinger proposed his cat paradox. The thought experiment suggested that a cat could exist in a state that is both alive and dead until it is observed. Schrödinger introduced the idea to highlight how strange quantum theory appeared.

Today, those once-bizarre concepts have moved far beyond philosophical debates.

Industry observers note that "That 'quantum weirdness' is no longer just a philosophical puzzle," remarked Scully. "It's the foundation of quantum computing, quantum cryptography and even gravitational wave detection.".

Industry observers note that the foundations of quantum mechanics were built by pioneers including Schrödinger and Werner Heisenberg. They developed two different mathematical approaches, wave mechanics and matrix mechanics, to describe quantum systems. Over time, these approaches were unified and contributed to the development of quantum field theory, which explains how particles interact through electromagnetic and nuclear forces.

Their work expanded on Niels Bohr's early atomic model, which pictured electrons orbiting the nucleus much like planets orbit the sun. While later discoveries refined that picture, Bohr's model helped pave the way for modern quantum theory.

Quantum Coherence and the Rise of Lasers.

Among the most important concepts in quantum mechanics is quantum coherence. This phenomenon allows particles such as atoms and photons to remain linked in a coordinated state, even across significant distances.

Quantum coherence led directly to the development of the laser, a technology that many once believed could never work. Today, lasers are used throughout modern society, from supermarket barcode scanners to vision correction procedures and advanced scientific instruments.

Coherence is also closely tied to quantum entanglement, the phenomenon that prompted Albert Einstein to describe it as "spooky action at a distance.".

Industry observers note that entanglement enables particles to share information through uniquely quantum properties. These effects form the basis of quantum encryption systems and improve the sensitivity of sophisticated instruments such as the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), which detects tiny ripples in spacetime.

Quantum Heat Engines Challenge Classical Limits.

One of the more surprising applications of quantum physics involves quantum heat engines.

Traditional engines are constrained by the Carnot Limit, which defines the maximum efficiency allowed by classical thermodynamics. Researchers have found that by exploiting quantum coherence, it may be possible to create engines that exceed those classical limits.

"It's a striking example of how quantum principles can rewrite the rules of classical physics," Scully said.

Quantum Biology, Gravity, and Turbulence.

The influence of quantum mechanics now extends far beyond physics.

In biology, techniques such as coherent Raman spectroscopy allow researchers to examine viruses and other structures at the nanoscale, providing valuable insights into the microscopic world.

In a recent development, quantum ideas are also shaping efforts to understand the universe itself. Scientists working on concepts such as string theory and quantum gravity are attempting to reconcile quantum mechanics with Einstein's theory of relativity, one of the biggest unsolved problems in modern physics.

Recent findings suggest that researchers are even applying quantum concepts to the long-standing challenge of understanding turbulence. The chaotic motion of air and fluids affects weather patterns, climate systems, and aircraft performance. By studying superfluid helium, a substance that displays unusual quantum behavior, scientists are uncovering patterns that could improve climate modeling, storm prediction, and aviation safety.

The Next Century of Quantum Discovery.

Despite a century of success, quantum mechanics continues to raise profound questions.

Can gravity be quantized (i.e., does gravity behave like other forces at the quantum level)? Could quantum computers transform medicine and materials science? What newly introduced insights about the universe might emerge from future quantum technologies?

Scully believes the search for answers is only beginning.

Industry observers note that "At the start of the 20th century, many thought physics was complete," he said. "Now, in the 21st century, we know the adventure is just beginning.".

Five Ways Quantum Mechanics Affects Everyday Life.

#195439. Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

Scientists discovered the brain doesn't make decisions the way we thought

📅 13 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence.
  • In a recent development, led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS).
  • The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists at the University of Illinois Urbana Champaign have uncovered evidence that could reshape how researchers think about both the brain and artificial intelligence. Their findings suggest that decision making begins much earlier in the brain than traditional theories propose, offering fresh ideas for designing future AI systems that are more capable and far more energy efficient.

In a recent development, led by electrical and computer engineering professor Yurii Vlasov at The Grainger College of Engineering, the research was published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Science (PNAS). The study points to an unexpected role for early sensory brain regions in decision making, challenging the long accepted view that decisions emerge only after information moves through a strict hierarchy of brain regions.

Rethinking How the Brain Makes Decisions.

The human brain is widely regarded as the most complex structure in the known universe. Scientists still do not fully understand how it works, which is why reverse engineering the brain was identified by the National Academy of Engineering in 2008 as one of the 14 grand challenges for engineering in the 21st century.

For decades, many artificial intelligence systems, including convolutional neural networks, have been inspired by the idea that the brain processes information in a one way sequence. According to this traditional model, sensory information travels upward through increasingly complex brain regions until it reaches the frontal cortex, where decisions are made.

Vlasov and other researchers have increasingly questioned whether that picture is complete.

Instead, they are exploring a model based on natural intelligence, which has been refined through evolution over hundreds of millions of years. In this framework, the brain does not rely only on a step by step flow of information. Decision making also depends on interconnected feedback loops that allow information to move in both directions between brain regions.

Because biological intelligence performs remarkably complex tasks while using far less energy than today's AI systems, understanding this architecture could help guide the development of future artificial intelligence.

"We want to learn from a billion years of evolution," Vlasov said. "How is that biological intelligence organized architecturally? Can we learn from the architectural side of the brain and emulate that to make AI more effective, less power hungry, and more intelligent than it presently is? In the level of decision-making, that's where current AI is lacking.".

Early Brain Regions Show Decision Making Activity.

To investigate how these processes work, the research team focused on the brain's earliest stages of sensing and perception.

The scientists recorded neural activity in mice as they navigated a virtual reality corridor and made perceptual decisions. They found evidence of decision related activity in the primary somatosensory cortex (S1), one of the brain's earliest sensory processing areas.

Rather than simply passing information forward, S1 appeared to be influenced by higher brain regions through feedback loops. This top down regulation suggests that decision making involves continuous communication across multiple brain areas instead of a simple one direction flow of information.

Industry observers note that "The neural code of the brain is still mostly an unknown language," Vlasov mentioned. "But this systems-level understanding can be viewed as a potential impact on how more efficient artificial neural networks can be built -- how the next generation of AI can be thought through. Maybe with these analogies that we learn from real brains, we can improve AI further.".

What the Findings Could Mean for Future AI.

The researchers emphasize that the study does not provide a blueprint for building better artificial intelligence. Instead, it offers newly introduced insights into how the brain organizes decision making that could eventually inspire future AI architectures.

According to recent reports, next, Vlasov and his team proposal to investigate the timing of these brain signals in greater detail. They also intend to develop upcoming technologies for measuring neural activity to better understand how feedback loops emerge and coordinate different levels of brain processing.

"By looking at the fast temporal dynamics of neural activity, maybe we can understand better how these feedback loops are engaged in making decisions," Vlasov said. "Maybe that's the approach that potentially uncovers these presently unknown mechanisms -- how these feedback loops are organized dynamically and how they form and shape different levels of processing. Maybe that can be implemented in new architectures for AI.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We sent 1,000 streaming calls at the same moment through three self-hosted LLM gateways: the Langfuse AI Gateway, the LiteLLM proxy and AcruxCore. Each gateway was limited to 2 CPUs. As shipped, Langfuse finished 261 of the 1,000 streams and LiteLLM finished 403. Neither failure came from the gateway's own code.

In a recent development, langfuse's failures came from Linux's open-file limit, which Docker sets to 1,024 by default. LiteLLM had that problem too, plus a second one: an empty key cache sent hundreds of database lookups at once, and the ones that waited longer than 10 seconds were rejected. This article shows how each failure looked, how we traced it to its cause, and the settings that fixed it.

This benchmark measured the resource consumption of three LLM gateways under scaling concurrent streaming loads.

Full latency, memory, and feature results are available in the Langfuse vs LiteLLM vs AcruxCore benchmark.

Industry observers note that first-token times are medians of the streams that succeeded. Up to 250 streams, every gateway succeeded. Then the errors started, and they did not look alike:.

Recent findings suggest that A 502 and a 503 point at different layers, so we expected two different causes. Two of the three turned out to share one cause.

It has been revealed that linux counts every network connection as an open file, and it caps how many open files one process may hold. The cap has two values. The soft limit is the cap that is in force now. The hard limit is the ceiling: a process may raise its own soft limit up to that value, and no further.

A streaming gateway holds two connections for each stream: one from the client, and one to the model provider. That makes about 1,000 open files at 500 streams, and about 2,000 at 1,000 streams. A gateway also needs a few more files for its database, its logs and its own libraries.

Docker on our machine gave every container a soft limit of 1,024 and a hard limit of 524,288. All three gateways received the same two numbers. What differed was how each program treats them when it starts:.

It has been revealed that node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup. The Rust and Python services keep 1,024, and neither project's Compose file sets a higher value. So the two gateways ran out of open files near 500 streams, which is the point where the errors started.

Recent findings suggest that the out-of-files error appeared as a failed connection, not as a clear message. The Langfuse gateway's logs revealed failed connections to OpenAI, and also failed connections to Langfuse's own web service, which the gateway asks to check each key. Both come from one cause: a process that cannot open another file cannot open another socket. Its client then receives a 502.

Recent findings suggest that read the limit the process actually has, not the one you think Docker gave it. Process 1 is usually the main process in a container:.

Industry observers note that if the gateway runs under a supervisor or several workers, check each worker's process ID instead of process 1. To see how close a process is to its limit under load, count its open file descriptors:.

Raise the limit for the gateway service in its Compose file. We used 65,536 for all three gateways:.

It has been revealed that the same ulimits block works on the LiteLLM service. On Kubernetes or another platform, check /proc//limits inside a running container rather than assuming a value.

Recent findings suggest that with the open-file limit raised, the Langfuse gateway finished all 1,000 streams. LiteLLM still returned 503 errors. To separate the two causes, we ran LiteLLM with one worker and only the open-file limit raised. All 500 streams succeeded in that ladder, but 595 of 1,000 failed with 503.

It has been revealed that the 503 message names the authentication database, so we read LiteLLM's logs and its source. The log gave the same reason for all 840 failed streams in these runs, 595 in that ladder and 245 in the cold-cache runs below:.

Three settings in LiteLLM explain it:.

According to recent reports, when 500 calls arrive while the key is not in the cache, each call looks the key up in Postgres. All of those lookups queue for 10 connections. The worker was also using its whole CPU allowance at this point, which slows every query it sends and receives. We infer that this CPU load lengthens the queue, but we did not measure it separately. Whatever the share of each, the lookups at the back of the queue miss the 10-second deadline.

It has been revealed that if that explanation is right, the failures should depend on whether the key is already in the cache. So we ran 500 streams four more times. Three runs started after 75 seconds with no calls, which is longer than the 60-second cache. One run started right after a single warm-up call:.

Sources indicate that the warm run had no failures. The cold runs failed by different amounts, 161, 84 and 0, because the result depends on how many lookups miss the deadline, and that changes from run to run. This probably explains why the earlier ladder succeeded at 500 and failed at 1,000. A run is a race between the lookup queue and the deadline, so a single ladder does not show where the limit is.

The warm-up result is the one we measured. Send one call with each virtual key after LiteLLM starts, and avoid quiet periods longer than 60 seconds before a traffic spike. A steady flow of traffic keeps the key in the cache.

LiteLLM also exposes three settings that act on this path. We did not test them, so treat them as places to look rather than proven fixes:.

Industry observers note that we raised the open-file limit to 65,536 for all three gateways and gave LiteLLM 2 workers, one per CPU, as its production guide recommends for a single machine. Then we ran the full ladder again:.

The open-file errors were gone for every gateway, and the Langfuse gateway gave the fastest first token of the three. LiteLLM still returned 120 × 503 at 500. That level started about 60 seconds after the first call of the ladder, so the cached key had probably just expired. All 1,000 succeeded at the next level, which started within 60 seconds of the 500 level.

Once nothing failed, CPU decided the first-token times. LiteLLM used its whole 2-CPU allowance from 100 streams on, and its median first token took 19.2 seconds at 1,000 streams. AcruxCore also used both CPUs from 100 streams on, and its first token at 1,000 streams was 3.8 s at the median and 9.7 s at p95. The Langfuse gateway peaked at 1.65 CPUs and 168 MiB, with a first token of 1.7 s at the median and 9.6 s at p95.

Each gateway also needs the rest of its stack, and that stack uses CPU too. While the Langfuse gateway served 500 streams, its whole stack used up to 3.1 CPUs, because the web service checked keys and the worker and ClickHouse stored usage. AcruxCore's whole stack peaked at 4.0 CPUs, because its API writes a trace for every call to Postgres. Size the stack around the gateway, not only the gateway container.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: Today, Meta releases Llama Guard 4, a 12B dense (not a MoE!) multimodal safety model, and two new Llama Prompt Guard 2 models. This release comes with multiple open model checkpoints, along with an interactive notebook for you to get started easily 🤗. Model checkpoints can be found in Llama 4 Collection.

In a recent development, vision and large language models deployed to production can be exploited to generate unsafe output through jail breaking image and text prompts. Unsafe content in production varies from being harmful or inappropriate to violating privacy or intellectual property.

Newly introduced safeguard models address this concern by evaluating image and text, and the content generated by the model. User messages classified as unsafe are not passed to vision and large language models, and unsafe assistant responses can be filtered out by production services.

Industry observers note that llama Guard 4 is a new multimodal model designed to detect inappropriate content in images and text, whether used as input or generated as output by the model. It’s a dense 12B model pruned from Llama 4 Scout model, and it can run on a single GPU (24 GB of VRAM). It can evaluate both text-only and image+text inputs, making it suitable for filtering both inputs and outputs of large language models. This enables flexible moderation pipelines where prompts are analyzed before reaching the model, and generated responses are reviewed afterwards for safety. It can also understand multiple languages.

The model can classify 14 types of hazard defined in the MLCommons hazard taxonomy, along with code interpreter abuse.

The list of categories detected by the model can be configured by the user on inference, as we’ll see later.

Llama Guard 4 employs a dense feedforward early-fusion architecture, in contrast to Llama 4 Scout, which uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers with one shared dense expert and sixteen routed experts per layer. To leverage Llama 4 Scout pre-training, the architecture is pruned into a dense model by removing all routed experts and router layers, retaining only the shared expert. This results in a dense feedforward model initialized from the pre-trained shared expert weights. No additional pre-training is applied to Llama Guard 4. The post-training data consists of multi-image training data up to 5 images and human-annotated multilingual data, previously used to train Llama Guard 3 models. The training data consists of 3:1 text-only to multimodal data.

Below you can find the performance of Llama Guard 4 compared against Llama Guard 3, the previous iteration of the safety model.

Recent findings suggest that the Llama Prompt Guard 2 series introduces two new classifiers with 86M and 22M parameters, focused on detecting prompt injections and jailbreaks. Compared to its predecessor, Llama Prompt Guard 1, this new version offers improved performance, a faster and more compact 22M model, tokenization resistant to adversarial attacks, and simplified binary classification (benign vs. malicious).

To use Llama Guard 4 and Prompt Guard 2, make sure you have hf_xet and the preview release of transformers for Llama Guard installed.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.
  • Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.

Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.

According to the BBC, the former Lapsus$ hacker has been released on license and given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including banning him from using Telegram and Discord.

“You are a very talented young man,” Mr Justice Turner told Kurtaj before warning him: “Don’t let this happen again.”.

Kurtaj made headlines in September 2022 when he hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 clips containing nearly an hour of GTA 6 gameplay, revealing Vice City and the game’s two protagonists long before its official announcement.

Remarkably, the teenager carried out the attack while on bail for other cybercrimes, using an Amazon Fire Stick, a television, and a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse from a Travelodge hotel.

He also attempted to blackmail Rockstar, threatening to release the game’s source code unless the developer contacted him.

Rockstar later revealed that the breach cost the company approximately $5 million to recover from, alongside thousands of hours of staff time.

In December 2023, Kurtaj was sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital after being deemed unfit to stand trial due to his autism.

At the time, the court heard that he remained highly motivated to commit further cybercrimes and could potentially hack Rockstar again.

However, a subsequent assessment found him fit to stand trial, and he was moved to a conventional prison in January 2026.

In a recent development, even while behind bars, Kurtaj made headlines again in March after allegedly using a smuggled phone to post about GTA 6. He later pleaded guilty to possessing a mobile phone in prison.

On November 16, Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the Rockstar hack and several other cybercrimes involving companies including Uber, Revolut, and BT/EE.

His release comes just days after GTA 6 officially launched on November 19, more than four years after his original attack.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has faced another wave of GTA 6 leaks from the anonymous Cyberleek in 2026, including gameplay footage and claims of access to development builds.

#195435. Latest Update: Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

Latest Update: Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

📅 14 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J.
  • Recent findings suggest that in his latest book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today.
  • "These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

Recent findings suggest that in his latest book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today.".

It has been revealed that denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant upcoming risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

It has been revealed that "Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions.".

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how').".

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it.".

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Why Human Knowledge Resists Encoding.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem.".

Sources indicate that computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

It has been revealed that "Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning states. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying.".

Sources indicate that according to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it.".

Context and Culture Shape Intelligence.

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Recent findings suggest that context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

Recent findings suggest that "When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

Recent findings suggest that "Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought.".

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding.

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

Sources indicate that "Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide.".

According to recent reports, he argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

It has been revealed that "Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

Industry observers note that "Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

According to recent reports, "Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences.".

Qwen-3 shows us that through the chat_template we can provide better flexibility, smarter context handling, and improved tool interaction. These improvements not only improve capabilities, but also make agentic workflows more reliable and efficent.

Is there any explanation for why this template sometimes uses bra and ket symbols like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, but then other times uses XML notation like and instead of <|think_start|> and <|think_end|>?

It strikes me as being inconsistent.

Recent findings suggest that the identifiers using bra and ket symbols are tokens, i.e. they are actually recognised and converted to a single "special" token by the tokenizer. For example, <|im_end|> is used as the EOS_TOKEN. (And, as an aside, you need to know this if you want to try fine-tuning these Qwen models, because you need to explicitly set eos_token='<|im_end|>' in your fine-tuning configuration.).

The XML-style identifiers are placeholders that define sections of the generated output. They are tokenized in the same manner as for any other text (i.e. they are probably converted to multiple tokens, but that depends on the vocabulary), they have no predetermined special meaning, and their use is learned by the model during training.

That remarked, the specific placeholders and are pretty standard across reasoning models.

According to Mexico News Daily, the suspect initially entered the store in the San Ramón neighborhood and asked a woman named Lidia about medication.

He returned minutes later wearing a mask and hoodie, demanding money from the register while threatening to use a weapon allegedly concealed in his backpack.

That’s when Lidia’s daughter rushed to help, grabbing the family’s cat and holding it directly toward the robber’s face.

Industry observers note that sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers initiative around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

According to recent reports, actual development rarely follows that initiative. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

In a recent development, developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

According to recent reports, historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Industry observers note that completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

According to recent reports, carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Industry observers note that interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production challenges. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Sources indicate that bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

According to recent reports, capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

Sources indicate that these records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual matter could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

It has been revealed that historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating fresh tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

For example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the fresh estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The newly introduced integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Recent findings suggest that inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying matter.

It has been revealed that research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

According to recent reports, start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

It has been revealed that avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

In a recent development, A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Sources indicate that consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

Industry observers note that the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

According to recent reports, teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

According to recent reports, suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

Sources indicate that A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

Recent findings suggest that in such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Recent findings suggest that historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Sources indicate that teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Industry observers note that production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Sources indicate that historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as notable inputs to sprint forecasting.

Industry observers note that when you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

According to recent reports, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

In a recent development, however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

In a recent development, timeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

It has been revealed that apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

In a recent development, sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a strategy, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Industry observers note that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

It has been revealed that 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

It has been revealed that bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

Industry observers note that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

It has been revealed that **3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Industry observers note that teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

Industry observers note that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

According to recent reports, 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Recent findings suggest that time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Recent findings suggest that technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves
