It has been revealed that AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

Recent findings suggest that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real customers can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

According to recent reports, the Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every proposal, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Recent findings suggest that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

According to recent reports, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

According to recent reports, glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

In a recent development, glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

Bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

It has been revealed that bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web intends run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

In a recent development, retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

According to recent reports, v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

In a recent development, v0's Free plan gives upcoming users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

Figma's Starter initiative is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real company data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

According to recent reports, three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Industry observers note that agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human people.

According to recent reports, building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

The caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

Neville Naidoo is a technology journalist covering AI, startups, and the digital economy, with a focus on how emerging technologies are constantly evolving and shaping our everyday life.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

In a recent development, both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

Industry observers note that as we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

That shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

It has been revealed that the clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:.

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

Industry observers note that the Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Sources indicate that diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:.

Industry observers note that choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

If you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling latest generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

The DRAM and NAND shortages have driven SSD prices through the roof, but we've still managed to track down some of the best Black Friday SSD deals around. There are several 1TB and 2TB NVMe SSDs on sale — by far the most popular capacities — for less than $0.15 per GB from brands like MSI, Adata, Biwin, and Kingston. Normally, we're using price per GB as our north star here to make sure you're getting the best value for the drive you pick up.

All of the drives we've rounded up here are PCIe 4.0 SSDs, and they range in performance. Short of one exception for the 1TB and 2TB capacities, these are DRAM-less SSDs. Naturally, SSDs with a DRAM cache are more expensive. There are good deals on high-end drives like the Samsung 9100 Pro 2TB at 49% off, but we're focused on value options here. If you need more capacity, the T-Force G50 Evo 4TB at $399 is the best deal we've found.

It has been revealed that A couple of the drives here are cheaper than when we reviewed them, in some cases a few years ago before the SSD pricing crisis took hold. Things are starting to turn in a positive direction with some of these discounts, though we still have a long way to go before we reach early 2025 pricing.

The Biwin Black Opal NV7400 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with maximum read speeds of up to 7,450 MB/s, and maximum write speeds of up to 6,500 MB/s.

The Biwin Black Opal NV7400 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD with maximum read speeds of up to 7,450 MB/s, and maximum write speeds of up to 6,500 MB/s.

Industry observers note that the headline deal is on the Biwin Black Opal NV7400, in both 1TB and 2TB capacities. It's a DRAM-less SSD, but it still boasts sequential reads/writes of up to 7,400 MB/s and 6,500 MB/s, respectively, and random reads/writes of 1,000K IOPS and 900K IOPS. It also comes with a generous five-year warranty and an endurance rating of 1PBW per TB of capacity.

We found that the drive was a solid all-around performer in our Biwin Black Opal NV7400 review. Prices on SSDs have continued to rise since we reviewed the NV7400 in January, but with current sales, the price on both the 1TB and 2TB versions of the NV7400 is still less than when we reviewed the drive.

Industry observers note that if you're looking for the cheapest 1TB NVMe SSD on Black Friday, the Kingston NV3 has the NV7400 beat out by $8. Both the 1TB and 2TB capacities are on sale, though the 1TB discount is the sweetheart deal right now. It too is a DRAM-less drive, and it comes with lower-rated specs than the NV7400 at 5,000 MB/s and 3,000 MB/s sequential reads and writes, and an endurance rating of 320 TBW for the 1TB capacity.

The Kingston NV3 is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that sports sequential read speeds of up to 6,000 MB/s and sequential write speeds of up to 4,000 MB/s.

According to recent reports, kingston's budget drives like the NV3 use somewhat of a grab bag approach to components, swapping out the controller and flash for whatever's available at the time. Compared to prior generations, the NV3 has stronger constraints to keep performance relatively comparable across different internal components. However, there can still be differences, as you can read about in our Kingston NV3 review.

Recent findings suggest that the MSI Spatium M470 Pro is a PCIe 4.0 NVMe SSD that supports sequential read speeds of up to 6,000 MB/s and sequential write speeds of up to 5,000 MB/s. $50 off w/ promo code BFF586.

It has been revealed that if you're looking for a drive that has a DRAM cache, you can save $50 on the 2TB MSI Spatium M470 Pro. The drive has 1GB of DDR4 per TB, 5,000 MB/s and 4,400 MB/s sequential read and write speeds, and 600,000 IOPS for random read/write performance. It also comes with a large 3,300 TBW endurance rating for the 2TB capacity, along with a five-year warranty.

The 2TB is actually $30 less than the list price when we reviewed it more than four years ago; check out our full MSI Spatium M470 review. Granted, PCIe 4.0 drives were more expensive four years ago than they were two years ago, but it's still a positive pricing move given how expensive SSDs have become.

The Adata Legend 860 is a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD with 6,000 MB/s and 5,000 MB/s sequential read/write performance and a three-year warranty.

In a recent development, rounding out the deals is the Adata Legend 860 1TB, which is an older PCIe 4.0 rated for 6,000 MB/s and 5,000 MB/s sequential read/write performance. It squarely clocks in at $0.15 per GB, and it's just $10 more expensive than the NV3 for the same capacity.

It's a DRAM-less drive, instead leveraging SLC caching and HMB, but it comes with a five-year warranty and a respectable 640 TBW endurance rating for the 1TB capacity.

Google this weekend rolled out the latest update to Pixel Weather with a new reporting feature and small interface tweaks.

Sources indicate that on the homepage, cities that have active weather warnings no longer have bright red card backgrounds. The pill-shaped container retains its Dynamic Color theming with just the text of the warning in red. This change also extends to the card on the city page. Finally, the source, like “Google Weather,” at the very bottom is now themed.

The main change today is a “Report current weather” feature to “Share the current weather condition to improve local forecasts.” The card appears at the very bottom of your current location and can be moved up the feed.

Google says to “Submit a report if the weather conditions don’t look right.” Tapping “Submit a report” brings up a “Report weather in [city]” sheet. You can submit two pieces of information:.

On the privacy front: “Your feedback, device location and some diagnostic information will be collected to help improve forecasts. This information will not be associated with your Google account.”.

This is rolling out with version 1.1.20261012.x of Pixel Weather that widely rolled out this weekend.
